Describing Student Growth
■ Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
 task.
■ Some believe a vertical scale simplifies the task of measuring
 student growth.
■ Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
■ Consider, for example, height.
 A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
 4 inches is a well understood quantity.
 The 4 inch increase becomes really meaningful only when understood alongside
 the growth of other 3 to 4 year olds.
■ Student growth percentiles were developed to provide a norm-
 referenced description of student growth (i.e., a growth norm).

SGPs maximize benefits and minimize weaknesses of student growth data

■ Prior to the SGPs,
 individuals had no easy way
 to determine if they
 performed better or worse on
 MCAS from one grade to the
 next
■ Change scores demonstrate
 regression to the mode
■ SGPs are strongly correlated
 with change (r = .85), but are
 more stable
■ SGPs are strongly
 associated with future
 performance on MCAS
■ SGPs are very weakly
 correlated with student
 demographics
■ Given MCAS’ lack of floor/
 ceiling effects, SGPs allow
 all students ~equal chance
 to grow
